questions.question: The Wall Street Crash came in October 1929, but the Depression deepened for years. What made it so severe?
options: Thousands of banks failed, wiping out ordinary savings
A drought destroyed the entire American wheat harvest
The government spent so heavily it triggered inflation
European nations called in all American war loans at once
questions.answer: Thousands of banks failed, wiping out ordinary savings
questions.explanation: Around 9,000 US banks failed between 1930 and 1933, and deposits were not insured, so people simply lost everything. Each failure destroyed money supply and credit, and fear of the next collapse caused runs on solvent banks too. Unemployment peaked near 25%. Roosevelt's first act in 1933 was closing every bank for four days, then reopening only the sound ones, which restored confidence almost immediately.
questions.memory_hook: About 9,000 banks failed between 1930 and 1933 with no deposit insurance, so savings simply vanished. Each collapse destroyed credit and triggered runs on healthy banks too. Unemployment hit 25%. Roosevelt shut every bank for four days and reopened only the sound ones, which worked almost instantly.

questions.question: Newton published his laws of motion in 1687. What did he do during the plague year of 1665?
options: Worked out calculus, optics and gravitation in isolation
Abandoned science entirely to concentrate on alchemy
Served as a physician inside the London plague hospitals
Fled to France and studied there under René Descartes
questions.answer: Worked out calculus, optics and gravitation in isolation
questions.explanation: Cambridge closed for plague and Newton went home to Woolsthorpe, where in roughly eighteen months he developed calculus, split light with a prism, and began the work on gravitation. He later called it his year of wonders. He then sat on most of it for two decades, publishing only when Halley pushed him. He also spent enormous effort on alchemy and biblical chronology, which he considered no less serious.
questions.memory_hook: Cambridge shut for plague, Newton went home, and in about eighteen months invented calculus, split light with a prism and started on gravity. His year of wonders. Then he sat on it for twenty years until Halley pushed him. He took his alchemy just as seriously.

questions.question: The Davis Cup is tennis's oldest international team event. What is unusual about its format?
options: Players compete individually and scores are combined
Matches are played over several days at a home venue
It is contested only in Olympic years
Only players under twenty-three may enter
questions.answer: Matches are played over several days at a home venue
questions.explanation: Traditionally a tie ran across three days at one nation's home ground, with the host choosing the surface to suit its own players, so Spain would pick clay and the US a hard court. Home crowds are far louder than at normal tournaments. The format was overhauled in 2019 into a centralised week-long finals event, which many players and fans disliked precisely because it removed the home-and-away element that made it distinctive.
questions.memory_hook: A tie ran three days at one nation's home ground, with the host picking the surface to suit itself, so Spain chose clay. Crowds were louder than normal tennis allows. It was overhauled in 2019 into a neutral week-long event, which removed the exact thing that made it special.

questions.question: Paul McCartney woke up with the melody for Yesterday already complete. What did he do next?
options: Wrote the lyrics first and fitted the tune afterward
Spent months asking people whether he had stolen it
Recorded it the same afternoon before he forgot
Gave it away to another artist before reclaiming it
questions.answer: Spent months asking people whether he had stolen it
questions.explanation: McCartney dreamt the melody and was convinced he must have heard it somewhere, playing it to people for weeks asking if they recognised it. The working lyric was scrambled eggs, oh my baby how I love your legs. It was recorded with McCartney alone on guitar and a string quartet, the first Beatles track with no other member on it. It is among the most covered songs ever written.
questions.memory_hook: He dreamt the tune and spent weeks playing it to people asking whether he had accidentally stolen it. The working lyric was scrambled eggs, oh my baby how I love your legs. Recorded with just McCartney and a string quartet, the first Beatles song with no other Beatle on it.

questions.question: The Trans-Siberian Railway is the world's longest railway line. Which two cities does it connect?
options: Moscow and Vladivostok
Moscow and Beijing
St. Petersburg and Tokyo
Kiev and Vladivostok
questions.explanation: The Trans-Siberian Railway stretches 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok on the Pacific coast — a journey of about 7 days covering 8 time zones. Completed in 1916, it was crucial for Russian expansion into Siberia and the Far East. A branch line extends to Beijing.
questions.memory_hook: Trans-Siberian: Moscow → Vladivostok. 9,289 km. 7-day journey across 8 time zones.

questions.question: The Rwandan genocide killed around 800,000 people in 100 days. How was killing organised so fast?
options: A standing army swept systematically through each province
Radio broadcasts named targets and directed local militias
Victims were transported to a small number of camps
Foreign mercenaries were hired to carry out the killings
questions.answer: Radio broadcasts named targets and directed local militias
questions.explanation: Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines broadcast dehumanising propaganda for months, then read out names and locations during the killing. Much of it was done by neighbours with machetes rather than soldiers, which is what made it so fast and so hard to stop. The UN force present was ordered not to intervene, and Western governments avoided the word genocide because using it would have triggered treaty obligations to act.
questions.memory_hook: A radio station spent months on dehumanising propaganda and then read out names and addresses during the killing. Much of it was neighbours with machetes, not soldiers, which is why it moved so fast. UN troops were ordered not to intervene, and governments dodged the word genocide to avoid the legal duty to act.

questions.question: The Simpsons has run since 1989. What did it start as?
options: A one-off Christmas special never meant to continue
Crude animated shorts on a sketch comedy show
A radio serial that ran for two years first
A newspaper comic strip syndicated nationally
questions.answer: Crude animated shorts on a sketch comedy show
questions.explanation: Matt Groening sketched the family in a lobby in fifteen minutes before pitching bumper shorts for The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987, naming them after his own family but substituting Bart for Matt. The early animation is notably rough. It became a half-hour series in 1989 and is now the longest-running American scripted primetime show. Groening had intended to pitch his existing comic strip and changed his mind rather than surrender the rights.
questions.memory_hook: Groening drew the family in a lobby in fifteen minutes for bumper shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987, naming them after his own family but swapping Bart for Matt. He was supposed to pitch his comic strip and changed his mind rather than hand over the rights.

questions.question: Frank Drake proposed his equation at the first SETI conference in 1961. What does it try to calculate?
options: How many communicating civilizations exist in our galaxy
The minimum technology level needed for radio contact
How long a signal takes to reach the nearest civilization
The odds a civilization survives its first 1,000 years
questions.answer: How many communicating civilizations exist in our galaxy
questions.explanation: N = R* × fp × ne × fl × fi × fc × L — the equation multiplies: rate of star formation, fraction of stars with planets, number of habitable planets per system, fraction where life emerges, fraction that develop intelligence, fraction that develop detectable technology, and average lifespan of such civilizations. The first few factors are now reasonably well-constrained by exoplanet surveys; the biological and cultural factors (fl, fi, fc, L) remain entirely unknown. The last term 'L' — how long civilizations last — may be the key: if most destroy themselves quickly, N approaches zero. Drake himself estimated about 10 civilizations in the Milky Way right now.
questions.memory_hook: The Drake Equation is essentially multiplication organized ignorance — most of its 7 factors are unknown. The most chilling term is 'L': how long does an intelligent civilization survive? If most destroy themselves quickly, the equation predicts we're alone. Drake himself estimated maybe 10 civilizations in the Milky Way.

questions.question: The Sahel sits between the Sahara and the savanna. What is the Great Green Wall meant to do there?
options: Divert water from the Congo to irrigate the region
Plant a belt of trees 8,000km across the continent
Build a physical barrier to stop sand blowing south
Relocate farming communities away from the desert edge
questions.answer: Plant a belt of trees 8,000km across the continent
questions.explanation: The African Union project aims to restore 100 million hectares in a band from Senegal to Djibouti. Progress has been slow and early plantings often died, since simply putting trees in arid ground rarely works. The approach has shifted toward supporting farmer-managed natural regeneration, protecting existing root systems so trees regrow on their own, which has proved far more effective and much cheaper in Niger and Burkina Faso.
questions.memory_hook: An 8,000km band of restored land from Senegal to Djibouti, aiming at 100 million hectares. Early plantings mostly died, because sticking saplings in dry ground does not work. The shift has been to protecting existing root systems so trees regrow themselves, which is cheaper and works better.

questions.question: The Black Death killed perhaps a third of Europe. What did it change for survivors?
options: Church attendance rose sharply and stayed high for centuries
Trade with Asia ceased entirely for over a hundred years
Labour shortages let peasants demand wages and mobility
Cities were abandoned permanently in favour of rural life
questions.answer: Labour shortages let peasants demand wages and mobility
questions.explanation: With so many dead, surviving workers were suddenly scarce and could bargain, which undermined serfdom across Western Europe. Governments tried to freeze wages by law and largely failed. Real wages rose substantially and stayed elevated for a century. The Church also lost authority, having proved unable to explain or stop it. Historians widely treat the plague as an accelerant of the transition out of the feudal order.
questions.memory_hook: So many died that surviving workers became scarce and could suddenly bargain, which broke serfdom across Western Europe. Governments tried to freeze wages by law and failed. Real wages stayed high for a century. The Church lost authority too, having neither explained nor stopped it.

questions.question: Beethoven wrote his Ninth Symphony while completely deaf. How did he manage that?
options: He could hear the music internally without external sound
He used a device that transmitted sound through his teeth
An assistant played passages and described them to him
He recovered partial hearing during the years of composition
questions.answer: He could hear the music internally without external sound
questions.explanation: Composition is largely mental for a trained musician, and Beethoven had internalised orchestral sound completely, so deafness cost him performance rather than composition. He did saw the legs off a piano to feel vibrations through the floor. At the Ninth's premiere in 1824 he was still beating time, out of sync with the orchestra, and a singer had to turn him around to see the audience applauding.
questions.memory_hook: Trained composers hear internally, so deafness cost him performing rather than writing. He did cut the legs off a piano to feel vibrations through the floor. At the Ninth's premiere he was still conducting, out of time, and a singer had to physically turn him round to see the applause.

questions.question: Roger Bannister broke the four-minute mile in May 1954. How long did his record survive?
options: Six years, until the Rome Olympics of 1960 came around
Forty-six days, before John Landy ran faster in Finland
Twelve years, standing until the middle of the 1960s
Two weeks, broken by one of his own pacemakers that month
questions.answer: Forty-six days, before John Landy ran faster in Finland
questions.explanation: Bannister ran 3:59.4 at Iffley Road, Oxford, paced by Chris Brasher and Chris Chataway. John Landy took the record 46 days later with 3:57.9. The two met that August at the Empire Games in Vancouver, the first race with two men under four minutes, and Landy glanced over his left shoulder on the final bend as Bannister passed him on the right. Bannister was a medical student training on lunch breaks and retired that year to practise neurology.
questions.memory_hook: Forty-six days, then John Landy beat it. They raced head to head that August in Vancouver, and Landy looked over his left shoulder exactly as Bannister came past on the right. Bannister was a medical student training on his lunch breaks, and quit running that year to become a neurologist.
